doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Day two: LA youth and army revisited
title: The leading drummers in LA when he was a kid
summary: He names Oscar Bradley, Lee Young, Red Alton and Wesley Prince as the top drummers, says he was the kid with little rapport with them, and recalls young drummers like Bill Douglas.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Sure, sure. Well let’s go back. You know, we talked about your early childhood and what it was like growing up in Los Angeles. A couple of things. You talked about Lee Young. Who were some of the other drummers that were around that you might -­
Oscar Bradley and Lee Young were the two number one drummers -- oh, Red Alton.
You know his daughter, Avria Redd who plays saxophone?

Vi Redd, right. Her father was a drummer. He had his own band, group, and Prince, Wesley Prince, I think that was his name, who was the brother of the bass player at that time that was with Nat Cole, with Nat. I can’t think of -- the early trio. But anyway those guys were -- they were the number one guys around town at that time, you know.
So you got a chance to see really good drummers.

Oh, yeah, very definitely, you know. But I didn’t have any kind of rapport with them though or they didn’t have any kind of rapport with me because I was -- you know, I was the kid, you know, that type of thing and it just -- coming up that way, the rapport I had was with guys like Jimmy Owens. We used to call Juicy. Hell, I can’t even think of him, Bill Douglas.

As a matter of fact I have a drum that Bill made for me, you know, and there weren’t that many drummers on the scene in LA at that time. Young guys, you know. And it was cool. And mainly, you know, like I said I was self-taught, just dug everything I could. You know, I would always try something.
